Posted March 8, 2001
Analysis by Richard Cowan

George Clemenceau famously said, " War is much too serious a matter to be entrusted to the military. " It is even more important that we recognize that the law is much too important to be entrusted to law enforcement. Indeed, if the definition of a " police state " is a state run by and for the police, it would be difficult to see how DEAland does not qualify for that label.

Presently, most of the state legislatures in DEAland are in session and the role of the police and prosecutors in shaping the laws that give them power is seldom viewed critically. On the contrary, police lobbyists are treated like experts on a wide variety of subjects that are really quite beyond their areas of competence.

Recently various law enforcement officials have testified about proposed medical marijuana and hemp cultivation bills.

In New Hampshire, Enfield Police Chief Peter Giese, representing the state’s Police Chiefs Association led his group’s opposition to a proposed medical marijuana bill.

" I am here because we believe this is nothing more than an entree into the legalization debate,'' Giese said. " This is a bill to legalize marijuana in the state of New Hampshire. ''

He went on to claim that the state would risk losing federal money because prescribing marijuana for medical use is against federal law. Of course, none of the states with medical marijuana laws have lost any federal funding. There is no such provision in any federal law. In fact, the various state medical marijuana laws do not require that doctors write a " prescription " -- but rather just some form of approval. In short, the representative of the New Hampshire Police Chiefs Association, which has no expertise in medicine, was lying about the law, which they should be expected to know – and to obey.

Is this acceptable behavior for " law enforcement? " Well, it is hardly unique.

Similar scenes have played out around the country. Police claim that they cannot tell a field of hemp stalks from marijuana, something that does not seem to be a problem in Canada or anywhere else.

State legislatures are accustomed to hearing self-serving testimony, but the police – of all groups – should not be allowed to lie with impunity while they are trying to maintain or increase their power.

Perhaps even worse, in California, much of the state’s law enforcement has simply refused to obey the state’s medical marijuana laws.
See
We Are Winning! Kubby Victory Forces California Politicians to Take Marijuana Issues Seriously. Paying a High Price for Not Paying Attention to Lawless Law Enforcement.

Consider the recent and very belated recognition that the DARE program doesn’t work and is probably even counterproductive. DARE is a product of the police establishment that has attacked DARE’s critics even after they knew that the critics were right.
See
Even The Prohibitionists Are Attacking DARE. What Is the Definition of Fraud? Analysis By Richard Cowan

The problem is not just that DARE is a fraud perpetrated by the police, although that point seems to have escaped most observers.

Consider that if the police could have been lying about DARE, mightn’t they be lying about other things as well? DARE is merely a small part of the much greater problem that law enforcement per se is an institutionalized fraud in most of the world. Although there are many competent individual police officers and well run forces, policing is not a science. Modern policing – like modern medicine – is the product of evolutionary processes that reflect the societies in which they operate. Police departments are organizations with notoriously closed cultures and institutional interests that make them very resistant to criticism, especially when there is power at stake.
See
Great Canadian Editorial Calls for Legalization; Decries Justice Minister's Giving Narks Veto Over Changing Marijuana Laws.

Theoretically, Grand Juries and prosecutors are supposed to protect the public from any abuses by the police. The fact is that this almost never happens. Instead, Grand Juries have become rubber stamps for prosecutors, who – in turn -- have come to depend on what they know is perjured testimony from the police and their informants.

To complete the corruption of the process, through the Mandatory Minimum laws which apply in many " drug " cases, the politically powerful prosecutors and their police allies have wrested control of the courts from the judges. Consequently, most drug cases never make it to trial because the prosecutors can extort plea bargains from defendants because the prosecutors – not the judges – control the sentencing process. The prosecutorial culture has become as closed and self-perpetuating as the police.
See
 " Win at All Cost " Series Documents Prosecutorial Abuses; Now What? Or So What?
and
The Kubbys and The Prosecutor – An Insight into Pathological Prosecution
and links

Although it should be obvious that a people should never blindly entrust their liberty and safety to those have power over them, we seem to have forgotten this most elemental caution. As the Romans asked, who will watch the watchman? It is quite clear that no one really is watching. But that may be changing.

Last month, USAToday reported that the Bush administration is considering a proposal to create a national law enforcement panel to examine racial profiling, excessive use of force and a range of other issues police officials say are undermining public trust in police.

What makes this all the more important is that the proposal came from the International Association of Chiefs of Police, one of the largest police lobbying groups in the U.S., and would address what it calls ``a serious gap developing between police agencies and communities.''

If International Association of Chiefs of Police recognize this problem, then these questions that I am raising cannot be " anti-police " -- and they are not. However, we need to take a very hard look at the entire criminal justice system, not just the abuses at the police level. I am certain, however, that any " national law enforcement panel " that does not deal with the need to end marijuana prohibition will fail in its mission. It is very unlikely that they will ever even consider it.

Of the various frauds perpetrated by law enforcement, none are more egregious than the fraud of marijuana prohibition. I have long thought that ending marijuana prohibition would be a catalyst that could bring about a reform of the criminal justice system. I still think that revealing this fraud will have a devastating effect on the police state.
See
Giuliani’s Police State – Like the Marijuana Prohibition That He Loves – Is A Counterproductive Fraud. 3 Articles.

Nonetheless, there is the danger that ending marijuana prohibition, which would end the state of hostility between law enforcement and tens of millions of citizens, including many in the politically powerful upper middle class, might give the police free rein to abuse members of weaker groups.

Societies need police because there are some very bad and dangerous people in this world. However, every society must keep a very close watch on the watchman for the very same reason, because there are some very bad and dangerous people in this world -- and they become infinitely more dangerous when they are acting under the cover of the law.
